At 4:17 every morning, the town’s clocks stopped.

No one knew why. The clocks in kitchens, classrooms, churches, pharmacies, station platforms, and abandoned factories all gave the same little shiver, clicked backward one minute, and froze. Digital clocks blinked 4:17. Watches lost their hands. The clock tower above Main Street stopped with its minute hand pointing toward the old cinema.

At first, people complained.

They called repairmen from the city. They replaced batteries, rewired circuits, polished gears, and blamed the weather. The repairmen left shaking their heads. “It’s not mechanical,” one said. “It’s not electrical either.”

Then the townspeople began to adapt.

They set their clocks five minutes fast before bed. They learned to wake when the darkness thinned. They carried pocket watches that worked perfectly until 4:16, then became warm and silent in their palms. Children whispered that the town belonged to someone else during that minute, someone who didn’t like being watched.

By day, life continued. The baker kneaded dough. The postman delivered letters. The mayor cut ribbons in front of buildings no one needed. But beneath everything ran the quiet knowledge that, each night, time itself reached a locked door and waited.

Mara first noticed the woman in the yellow coat on a Tuesday.

She was standing beneath the clock tower at 4:17, though Mara only knew this because the clock had stopped. The woman’s face was turned toward the cinema, where the red letters had long ago lost half their glow. She looked neither old nor young. Her yellow coat was buttoned to the throat, and rain glittered in her dark hair.

Mara watched from her bedroom window.

The woman lifted one hand.

Not a wave. A signal.

Mara stepped away from the glass.

She was thirty-two years old and had lived in the town all her life. She had been sensible in the way people became sensible when they had outlived everyone who once called them reckless. She paid her bills on time. She locked doors. She avoided unnecessary mysteries.

But the next morning, she found a yellow button on her windowsill.

It was small, round, and warm.

The following night, Mara waited.

At 4:16, she put on her coat and walked outside. The streets were silver with frost. Every house slept behind its curtains. Even the stray dogs had vanished.

The clock tower clicked.

4:17.

The woman stood beneath it.

“You came,” she said.

Her voice sounded like a remembered song.

“Who are you?”

The woman glanced toward the cinema. “You don’t remember me?”

“No.”

“That’s the problem.”

She began walking. Mara followed.

The cinema had been closed for twenty years, since the fire that destroyed the projection room. Its doors were chained, its windows painted black. Yet when the woman touched the handle, the chain fell loose.

Inside, the lobby smelled of dust, wet wool, and something sweet—popcorn, perhaps, from a summer long gone.

The woman led Mara through the ruined corridor to Theater Three. The screen was torn down the middle. Rows of seats waited beneath a ceiling stained by smoke.

“Sit,” the woman said.

Mara did.

The woman climbed onto the stage and raised both hands.

The projector began to run.

Light spilled across the wall.

At first there was only snow. Then an image appeared: a little girl in a red dress, standing beside a river. She was holding hands with another child, a boy with a crooked smile and one shoe untied.

Mara stopped breathing.

She knew the boy.

His name was Tomas. He had been her brother.

He had died when they were nine.

The film continued. Tomas and Mara raced along the riverbank. They built a dam from stones. They argued over a blue marble. Then the image changed.

A summer afternoon. The river swollen with rain. Tomas climbing onto a fallen tree. Mara shouting at him to come down.

The tree rolled.

The river took him.

Mara had remembered screaming. She had remembered her father carrying her home. She had remembered the funeral, the black clothes, the closed coffin.

But she had forgotten what came before.

Tomas had turned back.

He had seen something in the water.

A yellow coat.

The woman stood at the riverbank, beckoning.

Mara watched her brother step toward it.

“No,” Mara whispered.

On the screen, Tomas looked directly at the camera. Directly at her.

Then he smiled.

The film stopped.

The theater fell quiet.

“Who is she?” Mara asked.

The woman in the yellow coat stood below the screen. “The minute between things.”

“What does that mean?”

“She comes for what is unfinished.”

Mara thought of Tomas, of the blue marble, of the last words she had shouted at him: Go on, then. Go if you’re so brave.

“I blamed myself,” she said.

“You blamed yourself because it was easier than admitting you couldn’t save him.”

The woman reached into her pocket and took out a blue marble.

Mara began to cry.

“Can I see him?”

“For one minute.”

The clocks outside remained frozen. The town held its breath.

The woman pointed toward the screen.

Tomas stood there now, older than nine and younger than thirty-two. His hair was wet. His crooked smile had survived.

Mara ran to him.

They embraced, though she could feel the cold river between them.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

“For what?”

“For telling you to go.”

“You didn’t make the river.”

“I should have followed.”

“You did,” Tomas said. “You followed me every day. You just didn’t know where you were going.”

The minute was thinning. Mara could feel it slipping away, like sand through a fist.

“Are you happy?” she asked.

Tomas considered this. “I’m not where you are.”

“That wasn’t what I asked.”

He smiled again. “Yes.”

The woman in yellow lifted her hand.

Mara held her brother tighter.

“I love you,” Tomas said.

Then the projector clicked off.

Morning arrived all at once.

Mara woke in Theater Three with her cheek against a dusty seat. Sunlight entered through the broken roof. The woman was gone.

In her hand was the blue marble.

That evening, Mara placed it on her windowsill beside the yellow button.

At 4:16 the next morning, she stood beneath the clock tower. The town was silent. Frost covered the streets. For the first time in twenty-three years, Mara was not afraid of the minute.

The clock clicked.

4:17.

And somewhere inside the old cinema, a projector began to turn.
